sessions.last_message_preview:
I’d rank these as the best evidence chain:

1. **SD40 reporter degradation plus global proteomics** is the strongest direct link. SD40 was minimized to a 36-aa tag with potent PT-179-induced eGFP degradation, then tested across N- and C-terminal fusion proteins; in the same logic, PT-179 degraded SD40-eGFP without broadly degrading other detected proteins, unlike pomalidomide. See local paper [L84](/Users/shiyifan/Projects/Enana/TestData3/KnowledgeBase/papers.md/Continuous_evolution_of_compact_protein_degradation_tags_regulated_by_selective_molecular_glues/Continuous_evolution_of_compact_protein_degradation_tags_regulated_by_selective_molecular_glues.md:84) and [L86](/Users/shiyifan/Projects/Enana/TestData3/KnowledgeBase/papers.md/Continuous_evolution_of_compact_protein_degradation_tags_regulated_by_selective_molecular_glues/Continuous_evolution_of_compact_protein_degradation_tags_regulated_by_selective_molecular_glues.md:86).

2. **Full-length CRBN MG-PACE with negative selection, followed by HEK293T degradation assays**, is the best evolution-to-function bridge. The authors selected against glue-independent CRBN binding, evolved SD36, then showed full-length-CRBN-evolved variants triggered PT-179-dependent eGFP degradation; SD36 reached DC50 14.3 nM. See [L78](/Users/shiyifan/Projects/Enana/TestData3/KnowledgeBase/papers.md/Continuous_evolution_of_compact_protein_degradation_tags_regulated_by_selective_molecular_glues/Continuous_evolution_of_compact_protein_degradation_tags_regulated_by_selective_molecular_glues.md:78), [L80](/Users/shiyifan/Projects/Enana/TestData3/KnowledgeBase/papers.md/Continuous_evolution_of_compact_protein_degradation_tags_regulated_by_selective_molecular_glues/Continuous_evolution_of_compact_protein_degradation_tags_regulated_by_selective_molecular_glues.md:80), and [L82](/Users/shiyifan/Projects/Enana/TestData3/KnowledgeBase/papers.md/Continuous_evolution_of_compact_protein_degradation_tags_regulated_by_selective_molecular_glues/Continuous_evolution_of_compact_protein_degradation_tags_regulated_by_selective_molecular_glues.md:82).

3. **Endogenous SD40 tagging of PLK1 and BRD4** best shows the system works beyond overexpressed reporters. Prime editing installed SD40 into native loci, and PT-179 drove robust degradation of endogenous PLK1 and BRD4. See [L88](/Users/shiyifan/Projects/Enana/TestData3/KnowledgeBase/papers.md/Continuous_evolution_of_compact_protein_degradation_tags_regulated_by_selective_molecular_glues/Continuous_evolution_of_compact_protein_degradation_tags_regulated_by_selective_molecular_glues.md:88) and the Fig. 3 legend at [L94](/Users/shiyifan/Projects/Enana/TestData3/KnowledgeBase/papers.md/Continuous_evolution_of_compact_protein_degradation_tags_regulated_by_selective_molecular_glues/Continuous_evolution_of_compact_protein_degradation_tags_regulated_by_selective_molecular_glues.md:94).

sessions.title: I'm preparing next week's lab meeting. Can you find recent papers on molecular glue degraders, using my preferred journals as a preference, and give me a short shortlist with why each paper is relevant? Please do not download or save anything.
sessions.last_message_preview:
For a follow-up study, I’d treat the paper’s strongest evidence as an experiment chain, not a single assay: first prove the glue is selective, then show the evolved tag converts that selectivity into degradation, then validate at endogenous loci.

**Best Experiments**
1. **PT-179 orthogonality profiling vs pomalidomide**
   The baseline matters: PT-179 did not detectably degrade canonical IMiD neosubstrates across tested cells and caused only 3 differentially expressed genes in MM.1S cells, versus 1426 for pomalidomide, while still binding/engaging CRBN. This separates “selective glue” from “inactive compound.” [paper.md](/Users/shiyifan/Projects/Enana/TestData3/KnowledgeBase/papers.md/10.1126_science.adk4422/paper.md:57), [paper.md](/Users/shiyifan/Projects/Enana/TestData3/KnowledgeBase/papers.md/10.1126_science.adk4422/paper.md:61), [paper.md](/Users/shiyifan/Projects/Enana/TestData3/KnowledgeBase/papers.md/10.1126_science.adk4422/paper.md:63)

2. **Full-length CRBN MG-PACE with negative selection**
   The best design lesson is that selection architecture predicts degradation. They selected against ligand-independent CRBN binders using IMiD-binding-deficient CRBN, and CTD-only evolved SD20 failed in human-cell degradation, while full-length CRBN-evolved variants worked. For a follow-up, keep full-length E3 context and an explicit negative-selection arm. [paper.md](/Users/shiyifan/Projects/Enana/TestData3/KnowledgeBase/papers.md/10.1126_science.adk4422/paper.md:79), [paper.md](/Users/shiyifan/Projects/Enana/TestData3/KnowledgeBase/papers.md/10.1126_science.adk4422/paper.md:81), [paper.md](/Users/shiyifan/Projects/Enana/TestData3/KnowledgeBase/papers.md/10.1126_science.adk4422/paper.md:83)

3. **SD40 reporter degradation plus proteome-wide specificity**
   This is the cleanest selectivity-to-function bridge. SD40 was minimized to 36 aa and improved PT-179 degradation potency; multiple N- and C-terminal fusions degraded dose-dependently; PRKRA degraded within minutes; and PT-179 degraded SD40-eGFP without other significant hits among ~7800 detected proteins. [paper.md](/Users/shiyifan/Projects/Enana/TestData3/KnowledgeBase/papers.md/10.1126_science.adk4422/paper.md:85), [paper.md](/Users/shiyifan/Projects/Enana/TestData3/KnowledgeBase/papers.md/10.1126_science.adk4422/paper.md:87)

4. **Endogenous PLK1-SD40 and SD40-BRD4 knock-ins**
   This is the strongest functional validation because it leaves overexpression reporters behind. PT-179 degraded SD40-tagged PLK1 and BRD4 from native genomic loci, which is the right model for follow-up target biology. [paper.md](/Users/shiyifan/Projects/Enana/TestData3/KnowledgeBase/papers.md/10.1126_science.adk4422/paper.md:89)

5. **BLI/TR-FRET plus cryo-EM/mutational logic**
   These are the mechanistic bridge experiments: SD0 binds CRBN-pomalidomide but not CRBN-PT-179, while SD40 binds CRBN with PT-179 or pomalidomide; structures then explain how SD40 engages PT-179-bound CRBN, especially through CRBN NTD contacts and the F18/PT-179 morpholine interaction. [paper.md](/Users/shiyifan/Projects/Enana/TestData3/KnowledgeBase/papers.md/10.1126_science.adk4422/paper.md:93), [paper.md](/Users/shiyifan/Projects/Enana/TestData3/KnowledgeBase/papers.md/10.1126_science.adk4422/paper.md:103), [paper.md](/Users/shiyifan/Projects/Enana/TestData3/KnowledgeBase/papers.md/10.1126_science.adk4422/paper.md:109)

If your follow-up is cell-line focused, prioritize experiments 1, 3, 4, and 5. If you’re thinking about mouse systems or in vivo work, add the mouse CRBN evolution arm: SD56 gave stronger PT-179-dependent degradation in mouse 3T3 cells, while mouse Ba/F3 proteomics found no broad PT-179 neosubstrate effect. sessions.last_message_preview:
**Constraints Mentioned**

From the loaded `source_lines`, the paper says broader anti-PD-1/PD-L1 therapy is constrained by:

- **Large antibody size** and **poor tumor penetration**: full-length antibodies are about 150 kDa and “do not readily penetrate tumors” (line 34).
- **Systemic toxicity**: systemic antibodies have long half-lives and can cause immune-related adverse events, including colitis and pneumonitis (line 34).
- **High production/manufacturing cost**: the abstract cites “high production costs” (line 24), and the comparison table says commercial mAbs can cost much more to produce than scFvs (line 159).
- **Interpatient variability**: response differs across patients, limiting more widespread use (line 34).
- **Off-tumor toxicity**: Fc-mediated ADCC and other effector functions may contribute to toxicities outside the tumor, especially in non-responders (line 34).
- **High systemic exposure and repeated dosing**: IV full-length anti-PD-1 mAbs lead to high circulating antibody levels, poor tumor penetration, variable responses, significant immune-related adverse events, and repeated dosing (line 139).
- **scFv-specific limitations**: short serum half-life, aggregation tendency, and possible immunogenicity (line 36).
- **Delivery-platform constraints**: payload stability, nanoformulation scalability, ADC stability, linker chemistry, and reproducible nanoparticle manufacturing (lines 65, 67).
- **Viral-vector constraints**: host antiviral immune responses, difficulty controlling replication kinetics, and off-target infection risk in non-tumor tissues (line 95).

sessions.last_message_preview:
Based on the transformed `paper.md`, the practical protocol is best treated as an end-to-end workflow for discovering and validating PT-179-responsive compact degrons, then using SD40 for inducible degradation.

**Protocol: SD40/PT-179 Inducible Degron Workflow**

**Materials**
- `S2060` and `S2208` E. coli strains; MP6 mutagenesis plasmid; MG-PACE accessory plasmids encoding CRBN or CRBNCTD selection circuits.
- Selection phage carrying evolving ZF degron variants in place of `gIII`.
- DRM/2xYT/LB media; arabinose, glucose, PMBN, DMSO, antibiotics.
- PT-179, PK-1016, pomalidomide, or other IMiD derivatives.
- HEK293T, K562, NIH 3T3 as needed; DMEM or RPMI + 10% FBS.
- Lentiviral reporter vector, `psPAX2`, `pMD2.G`, Lipofectamine 2000, polybrene, puromycin.
- Prime editor plasmid, pegRNAs/nicking sgRNA, MiSeq genotyping reagents.
- Flow cytometer and/or immunoblot reagents.

**Timing**
- Circuit validation: ~3 days.
- PANCE stepping-stone evolution: ~4 to 6 days for 8 to 9 passages.
- PACE evolution: ~6 to 12 days depending on run length.
- Lentiviral reporter generation/selection: ~1 week.
- Flow degradation assay: 2 days.
- Prime editing pool: 3 to 4 days; clonal line isolation: usually 2 to 4+ weeks.

**Step-by-Step**
1. Build the MG-PACE circuit. Fuse CRBN or CRBNCTD to the DNA-binding component and the evolving ZF degron to the RNAP omega component so ternary complex formation drives `gIII` or `luxAB` expression. The paper used SD0 as the starting degron and evolved toward PT-179-bound CRBN recognition.

2. Validate the selection circuit by luminescence. Transform `S2060`, grow colonies overnight, back-dilute 1:100, grow to OD600 0.3 to 0.4, add PMBN, add DMSO or compound, incubate ~1 hour at 37°C, then read OD600 and luminescence. Normalize luminescence to OD600.

3. Run PANCE for weak starting activity. Transform `S2060` with AP + MP6, induce mutagenesis with 10 mM arabinose, split into 1 mL cultures, add IMiD derivative, infect with phage, grow 8 to 16 hours, pellet cells, harvest supernatant, titer phage, and passage. The paper used 8 to 9 passages to find stepping-stone variants.

4. Run PACE for stronger selection. Seed chemostats with log-phase cells, maintain OD600 ~0.8 to 1.0, connect 3 to 15 mL lagoons supplied with arabinose, PMBN, and IMiD derivative. Pre-propagate phage in `S2208` + MP6 for 4 to 6 hours, infect lagoons with 150 uL phage, sample 500 uL over time, titer, and Sanger sequence plaques.

5. Increase stringency as variants improve. The paper used weaker `gIII` RBSs, lower compound concentration, full-length CRBN selection, and negative selection against ligand-independent CRBN binding. A key caveat is that variants evolved only on CRBNCTD may activate the bacterial circuit but fail in mammalian degradation assays.

6. Clone candidate degrons into mammalian reporters. Codon-optimize ZF variants and clone into a lentiviral reporter such as degron-eGFP-IRES-mCherry or degron-tagged target fusions.

7. Produce lentivirus in HEK293T cells. Seed 7.0e5 cells/well in a 6-well plate, transfect transfer vector + `psPAX2` + `pMD2.G`, change media after 5 to 6 hours, harvest and 0.45 um-filter supernatant after 48 hours.

8. Transduce reporter cells at low MOI. Infect HEK293T or NIH 3T3 cells with polybrene, keep MOI <=0.3, replace media the next day, select with puromycin for at least 3 days.

9. Measure degradation by flow cytometry. Plate selected cells in poly-D-lysine 48-well plates, treat next day with DMSO or compound at 0.5% final DMSO, incubate >=20 hours, then measure eGFP and mCherry. Analyze single-cell eGFP:mCherry geometric mean and normalize to DMSO.

10. Install SD40 endogenously by prime editing. For HEK293T pool testing, seed 15,000 cells/well in 96-well plates; after 16 to 20 hours transfect prime editor plus two pegRNAs; culture 4 days, extract genomic DNA, and quantify knock-in/indels by amplicon sequencing. For clonal PLK1-SD40 or BRD4-SD40 lines, single-cell clone after editing and screen colonies.

11. Confirm endogenous degradation by immunoblot. Plate 1.6e5 cells/well in 24-well plates, treat with DMSO or PT-179 at 0.5% final DMSO. Use 24 hours for most targets; the paper used 2 hours for endogenous PLK1-SD40. Lyse in RIPA, quantify protein, run SDS-PAGE, transfer, blot target/tag plus GAPDH or tubulin.

**Controls**
- DMSO vehicle.
- Pomalidomide positive control, with awareness of off-target neosubstrates.
- SD0 or nonresponsive degron negative control.
- Untagged target or unedited parental cells.
- mCherry internal expression control for flow assays.
- Biological triplicates for degradation curves.
- Editing controls: no editor, no pegRNA, and amplicon sequencing for correct edit vs indels.

**Key Caveats**
- Exact plasmids, degron sequences, pegRNAs, and donor designs depend on the paper’s supplementary tables/Addgene materials.
- PT-179 was synthesized in the study; sourcing and QC matter.
- Use full-length CRBN selection for variants intended to degrade proteins in cells.
- SD40 is optimized for human CRBN; the paper evolved SD56 for mouse cells.
- Prime editing efficiency is target- and cell-type-dependent; clonal screening is usually required.
- Lentivirus work requires the appropriate institutional biosafety setup.

sessions.title: What is nanobody
sessions.last_message_preview:
A nanobody is a very small antibody fragment that can still bind a specific target, like a protein or virus surface.

More precisely:
- It is usually derived from the single-domain antibodies naturally found in camelids such as llamas and alpacas.
- Unlike conventional antibodies, which have multiple chains, a nanobody is just the binding domain, so it is much smaller and simpler.
- Because of that, nanobodies are often easier to engineer, more stable, and better at reaching tight or hidden binding sites.

They are commonly used in:
- Research, for detecting or manipulating proteins
- Diagnostics
- Therapeutics, including some antiviral and anticancer applications

sessions.title: Can you generate a protocol to make competent cells?
sessions.last_message_preview:
Below is a standard protocol for preparing electrocompetent `E. coli` from a routine cloning strain such as `DH5alpha`, `TOP10`, `10-beta`, or `XL1-Blue`. I’m assuming a 1 L prep and a standard glycerol-wash workflow.

**Protocol**

1. Prepare and pre-chill everything before the harvest step: sterile water, sterile `10%` glycerol, centrifuge bottles, tubes, and rotor. After the culture is chilled, keep the cells at `0-4 C` throughout.
2. Start an overnight culture from a single colony in `5-10 mL` LB at `37 C` with shaking.
3. The next day, inoculate `1 L` fresh medium in a large flask `1:100` with the overnight culture and grow at `37 C` with shaking to `OD600 0.45-0.55`. Do not let the culture overgrow.
4. Chill the culture on ice for `10-15 min`.
5. Pellet the cells at `4 C` using a gentle spin such as about `3000 x g` for `10 min`. Decant the supernatant completely.
6. Gently resuspend the pellet in `500 mL` ice-cold sterile water. Spin again at `4 C` and discard the supernatant.
7. Resuspend in `250 mL` ice-cold sterile water. Spin again and discard the supernatant.
8. Resuspend in `50 mL` ice-cold sterile `10%` glycerol. Spin again and remove the supernatant as completely as possible.
9. Resuspend the final pellet in `1-2 mL` ice-cold sterile `10%` glycerol. Use the smaller volume if you want more concentrated cells.
10. Aliquot into pre-chilled tubes, typically `40-50 uL` per tube.
11. Freeze immediately in a dry ice/ethanol bath and store at `-80 C`.

**Optional QC Transformation**

1. Thaw one aliquot on ice.
2. Add clean plasmid DNA in water or low-salt buffer. For `25-50 uL` cells, keep DNA volume small, ideally `1 uL`, and not more than about `2.5 uL`.
3. Transfer to a pre-chilled `1 mm` cuvette without bubbles.
4. Pulse at `2.1 kV`, `100 ohm`, `25 uF`. A typical time constant is around `2.6 ms`.
5. Immediately add `975 uL` warm SOC, transfer to a tube, and recover at `37 C` for `1 h`.
6. Plate on pre-warmed selective agar.

**Notes**

- The two main failure modes are warming the cells and carrying over salt.
- If you see arcing, the DNA is usually too salty, there is residual medium in the cell prep, or there are bubbles in the cuvette.
- If efficiency is poor, first check growth phase. Harvesting outside mid-log commonly hurts performance.
- For library work or difficult strains, I would tighten this into a strain-specific protocol rather than use this generic version.

This is a standard protocol synthesized from the classical Dower electroporation workflow, current NEB electroporation guidance, and a widely used community prep workflow: [Dower et al., 1988](https://academic.oup.com/nar/article/16/13/6127/1046461), [NEB Electroporation Tips](https://www.neb.com/en/tools-and-resources/usage-guidelines/electroporation-tips), [NEB Electroporation Protocol](https://www.neb.com/en/protocols/0001/01/01/electroporation-protocol-c2986?pdf=true), and [OpenWetWare prep workflow](https://openwetware.org/wiki/Preparation_of_Electroporation-Competent_E._coli_Cells).

If you want, I can rewrite this as a tighter `50-100 mL` mini-prep version or adapt it for a specific strain.

sessions.title: Can you write a code in python to translate a fastq to amino acid sequence?
sessions.last_message_preview:
Yes. This version translates each FASTQ read independently, ignores quality scores, trims incomplete trailing codons, and writes protein sequences in FASTA format.

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3

import argparse
import gzip
import sys

CODON_TABLE = {
    "TTT": "F", "TTC": "F", "TTA": "L", "TTG": "L",
    "TCT": "S", "TCC": "S", "TCA": "S", "TCG": "S",
    "TAT": "Y", "TAC": "Y", "TAA": "*", "TAG": "*",
    "TGT": "C", "TGC": "C", "TGA": "*", "TGG": "W",
    "CTT": "L", "CTC": "L", "CTA": "L", "CTG": "L",
    "CCT": "P", "CCC": "P", "CCA": "P", "CCG": "P",
    "CAT": "H", "CAC": "H", "CAA": "Q", "CAG": "Q",
    "CGT": "R", "CGC": "R", "CGA": "R", "CGG": "R",
    "ATT": "I", "ATC": "I", "ATA": "I", "ATG": "M",
    "ACT": "T", "ACC": "T", "ACA": "T", "ACG": "T",
    "AAT": "N", "AAC": "N", "AAA": "K", "AAG": "K",
    "AGT": "S", "AGC": "S", "AGA": "R", "AGG": "R",
    "GTT": "V", "GTC": "V", "GTA": "V", "GTG": "V",
    "GCT": "A", "GCC": "A", "GCA": "A", "GCG": "A",
    "GAT": "D", "GAC": "D", "GAA": "E", "GAG": "E",
    "GGT": "G", "GGC": "G", "GGA": "G", "GGG": "G",
}

RC_TABLE = str.maketrans("ACGTNacgtn", "TGCANtgcan")


def open_text(path, mode="rt"):
    if path.endswith(".gz"):
        return gzip.open(path, mode)
    return open(path, mode)


def reverse_complement(seq):
    return seq.translate(RC_TABLE)[::-1]


def translate_dna(seq, frame=1, remove_stops=False):
    seq = seq.upper()
    start = frame - 1
    aa = []

    for i in range(start, len(seq) - 2, 3):
        codon = seq[i:i + 3]
        aa.append(CODON_TABLE.get(codon, "X"))

    protein = "".join(aa)
    if remove_stops:
        protein = protein.replace("*", "")
    return protein


def fastq_reader(handle):
    while True:
        header = handle.readline()
        if not header:
            break

        seq = handle.readline().strip()
        plus = handle.readline()
        qual = handle.readline().strip()

        if not plus or qual is None:
            raise ValueError("Malformed FASTQ: incomplete 4-line record")

        if not header.startswith("@"):
            raise ValueError(f"Malformed FASTQ header: {header.strip()}")

        if not plus.startswith("+"):
            raise ValueError(f"Malformed FASTQ separator: {plus.strip()}")

        yield header[1:].strip(), seq, qual


def main():
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(
        description="Translate FASTQ reads into amino acid sequences."
    )
    parser.add_argument("input_fastq", help="Input FASTQ file (.fastq or .fastq.gz)")
    parser.add_argument(
        "-o", "--output",
        default="-",
        help="Output FASTA file (default: stdout)"
    )
    parser.add_argument(
        "--frame",
        type=int,
        choices=[1, 2, 3],
        default=1,
        help="Reading frame to use (default: 1)"
    )
    parser.add_argument(
        "--revcomp",
        action="store_true",
        help="Translate the reverse-complement strand"
    )
    parser.add_argument(
        "--remove-stops",
        action="store_true",
        help="Remove stop codons (*) from protein output"
    )

    args = parser.parse_args()

    out_handle = sys.stdout if args.output == "-" else open(args.output, "w")

    try:
        with open_text(args.input_fastq, "rt") as in_handle:
            for read_id, seq, _qual in fastq_reader(in_handle):
                if args.revcomp:
                    seq = reverse_complement(seq)

                protein = translate_dna(
                    seq,
                    frame=args.frame,
                    remove_stops=args.remove_stops
                )

                out_handle.write(f">{read_id}\n{protein}\n")
    finally:
        if out_handle is not sys.stdout:
            out_handle.close()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

Example usage:

```bash
python fastq_to_aa.py reads.fastq -o proteins.fasta
python fastq_to_aa.py reads.fastq.gz --frame 2 --remove-stops -o proteins.fasta
python fastq_to_aa.py reads.fastq --revcomp
```

Important caveat: this is only biologically meaningful if your reads are already in the correct coding orientation and frame. If you want, I can also give you a version that uses `Biopython`, keeps only high-quality reads, or translates all 6 reading frames.

sessions.title: What is mRNA display
sessions.last_message_preview:
mRNA display is an `in vitro` directed-evolution method that physically links each peptide or protein to the `mRNA` that encodes it.

The key idea is `genotype-phenotype coupling`:
- the `protein/peptide` is what you want to test
- the attached `mRNA` tells you its sequence

It usually works by attaching `puromycin` to the mRNA. During translation, puromycin causes the newly made peptide to become covalently linked to its own mRNA. That lets you screen enormous libraries, keep the molecules with the property you want, then recover and amplify the matching sequences.

Typical workflow:
1. Make a large DNA library.
2. Transcribe it to mRNA.
3. Attach a puromycin-containing linker.
4. Translate in a cell-free system so each product links to its own mRNA.
5. Select molecules that bind a target or show some activity.
6. Recover, reverse-transcribe, and amplify the winning sequences.
7. Repeat for enrichment.

Why it is useful:
- supports very large libraries, often larger than cell-based display methods
- fully cell-free
- good for evolving binders, enzymes, and peptide therapeutics

sessions.title: What is phage display
sessions.last_message_preview: Phage display is a molecular biology technique that presents a peptide or protein on the surface of a bacteriophage while the DNA encoding it is carried inside the same phage. That links binding behavior to sequence, so you can screen a large library of variants, select the phage that bind a target through repeated rounds of biopanning, and then identify the enriched sequences. It is widely used for antibody discovery, epitope mapping, and finding peptides or proteins that bind specific molecules.

sessions.title: What is B cell leukimia
sessions.last_message_preview:
If you mean "B-cell leukemia," it is a blood cancer involving B cells, a type of white blood cell that normally makes antibodies. In this disease, abnormal B cells grow out of control in the bone marrow and blood and can crowd out normal blood cells.

"B-cell leukemia" is not just one disease. It can refer to different B-cell leukemias, especially:
- B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (B-ALL), which is fast-growing.
- Chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL), which usually grows more slowly.

Common symptoms can include fatigue, frequent infections, easy bruising or bleeding, swollen lymph nodes, fever, and weight loss. Diagnosis is usually made with blood tests and often a bone marrow test.

sessions.title: What is antibody
sessions.last_message_preview: An antibody is a Y-shaped immune protein made by B cells that specifically recognizes and binds a target, usually part of a virus, bacterium, toxin, or other foreign substance called an antigen. Antibodies help protect the body by neutralizing threats, blocking their activity, or marking them for destruction by other immune cells.
